summary: Discusses and defines terms used when describing performance benchmark tests for network interconnection devices and their results. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If you are going to race, you need to agree on what words like "fast" mean. This lists the words.

questions: how is latency defined for network devices
subtitle: A shared vocabulary so vendors measure and report network device performance in comparable ways.

tldr.problem: Vendors of network devices often play 'specsmanship', reporting performance numbers in confusing ways that buyers cannot compare.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines 17 terms, such as throughput, latency and frame loss rate, each with a definition, discussion, measurement units, issues and cross references.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that sets up later benchmarking memos, which were to define specific tests and a format for reporting results. It is updated by RFC 6201.

today: RFC 1242 is an Informational memo and is updated by RFC 6201. It defines terms only; the specific tests and reporting formats were left to follow-up memos.

sections.title: Why Benchmarking Terms Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 1242 comes from the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG) of the IETF. It begins with a frank complaint: vendors often engage in specsmanship, using much 'smoke and mirrors' to give their products a better position in the marketplace.

The memo and its follow-ups try to define a specific set of terminology and tests that vendors can use to measure and report the performance of network devices. The goal is to give the user comparable data from different vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every toy shop measured its toy cars in different ways and then shouted that theirs was best. This memo says: let us all use the same ruler.

sections.title: How Each Term Is Defined
sections.content:
Every term follows the same template. It has a Definition, a Discussion of the term and any limits on how to measure it, the Measurement units used to report it, a list of Issues that affect it, and a See Also list of related terms.

Some terms are about the kind of device being tested. A bridge forwards frames using data link layer information. A router forwards frames using network layer information, which implies running the routing algorithm and, for example, decrementing the TTL field. A bridge/router can act as either, depending on the protocol of each frame.
sections.plainLanguage: Each word gets the same little card: what it means, why it matters, how to count it, and which other cards to look at.

sections.title: Frames, Load and Timing Terms
sections.content:
Several terms pin down exactly what is being counted. Data link frame size is the number of octets from the first octet after the preamble to the end of the FCS, if present, or to the last octet of data if there is no FCS. The memo notes that authors disagree on whether to include the checksum, so it picks one definition.

Inter Frame Gap is the delay from the end of one frame, as defined above, to the start of the preamble of the next. A Constant Load is fixed length frames at a fixed interval, and the memo admits that a steady load is rare in the real world but useful for comparing devices. Back-to-back means fixed length frames sent with the minimum legal separation for the medium, starting from an idle state. It is used to learn how much data buffering a device has, for example for NFS-style transfers of up to 64K octets that become many fragments on Ethernet, or routing updates that span many frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you time a runner you must say where the starting line is. These words say exactly where a frame starts and ends and how fast they are sent.

sections.title: Throughput, Loss and Latency
sections.content:
Throughput is the maximum rate at which none of the offered frames are dropped by the device. It is reported as N-octet input frames per second or input bits per second, over an assortment of frame sizes, with separate figures for routed and bridged data in devices that do both. If frames carry a checksum, full checksum processing must be done.

Frame Loss Rate is the percentage of frames that should have been forwarded under steady load but were dropped for lack of resources. It is reported as a graph of offered load against frame loss.

Latency depends on the device type. For store and forward devices it runs from when the last bit of the input frame reaches the input port to when the first bit of the output frame is seen on the output port. For bit forwarding devices it runs from the end of the first input bit to the start of the first output bit. A 'cut through' device that starts sending early is still treated as store and forward, so its latency can even be negative.
sections.plainLanguage: Throughput is the fastest a conveyor belt can run without dropping any boxes. Frame loss is how many boxes fall off when you run it too fast. Latency is how long one box takes to get across.

sections.title: How Devices Behave Under Stress
sections.content:
The remaining terms describe behavior rather than a single number. Link Speed Mismatch is a mismatch between input and output data rates, for example an Ethernet on one side and a 56KB serial link on the other, also called the 'fire hose effect'. MTU-mismatch behavior covers an output network with a smaller MTU than the input network, which forces fragmentation.

Overhead behavior is processing other than for normal data frames, such as handling routing updates or management requests. Overloaded behavior is what happens when demand exceeds resources, and the memo treats any frame loss as an overloaded state. Policy based filtering is discarding frames by administrative decision, Restart behavior is the data loss and downtime after a power up or reset, and Single frame behavior is how a device handles one frame in isolation, which can take much longer than the same frame in a steady stream because of work such as ARP and cache setup.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tests ask how a machine acts when things go wrong: when it is rebooting, when it is swamped, or when the first item arrives and nothing is ready yet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states only that security issues are not discussed in it. It defines vocabulary and does not specify a protocol or an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This list of words is not about locks and keys, so the memo says nothing about safety.
